# Independent audit of the sharp simplex vertex-averaging coupling

Source: sharp-simplex-vertex-averaging-convex-order-coupling.md.

**Final verdict: PASS after the optional Section 5 scope repair.**
The main theorem in Sections 1–4 independently passes unchanged. The sharp
range is \(0\le b\le1/d\), where \(d\ge2\) is the number of
barycentric coordinates and the simplex has dimension \(d-1\).
The proof below independently verifies all probability factors and
the martingale. An optional Section 5 claim initially omitted the
zero-step atom; its exact correction is recorded in Section 5 of
this audit. The author has applied the repair, explicitly restricting
uniqueness to absolutely continuous step laws and recording the
zero-step mixtures. The corrected statement and its additivity
proof pass.

The companion verifier
supporting computation verify_sharp_simplex_vertex_averaging_convex_order.py was read and
rerun: **PASS 3189 exact checks, including 325 reconstructed moment
identities**. The proof, rather than those finite moments, establishes
the law identities and all-dimensional convex order.

## 1. Random-step uniformity and conditional expectation

In \(m\) coordinates, condition on a chosen vertex \(j\) and a step
\(r\). The image of the uniform simplex under
\(w\mapsto(1-r)w+r e_j\) has density
\((1-r)^{-(m-1)}\mathbf 1_{\{x_j\ge r\}}\) relative to uniform
simplex probability. Integrating against
\(m(1-r)^{m-1}dr\) gives \(m x_j\). Averaging over the \(m\)
vertices yields density one.

The same random step has mean \(1/(m+1)\), so
\[
\mathbb E[(1-R)W+R e_J\mid W,J]
=\frac m{m+1}W+\frac1{m+1}e_J.
\]
Conditioning further on the right-hand vector proves the martingale
property. This is a direct density calculation; no unproved
Dirichlet or convex-order assertion is needed. For \(m=1\), both
vectors are the single point of the zero-dimensional simplex.

## 2. Exact minimum-cell disintegration

At \(b=1/d\), write \(\rho=(d-1)/d\). The averaged affine images
have density
\[
f(y)=\frac{\#\{j:y_j\ge1/d\}}{d\rho^{d-1}}
\]
relative to the uniform \((d-1)\)-simplex. In particular the law
is absolutely continuous; all ties and threshold-boundary choices
are null.

On the cell whose unique minimum occurs at \(i\), put
\[
y_i=t/d,\qquad y_j=t/d+(1-t)w_j\quad(j\ne i).
\]
Under uniform probability the cell has mass \(1/d\), \(t\) has
density \((d-1)(1-t)^{d-2}\), and \(w\) is independently uniform
on the simplex with \(d-1\) coordinates. For example this follows
in a coordinate volume chart from the Jacobian
\((1-t)^{d-2}/d\); normalized full and lower-simplex densities
then give the stated cell mass and Beta law.

For \(t<1\), the minimum coordinate cannot be at least \(1/d\),
and the other threshold tests are exactly \(w_j\ge1/d\). Thus
the density factor depends on \(w\) alone. Its normalizing
denominator is
\[
d\rho^{d-1}=(d-1)\rho^{d-2},
\]
which is exactly the denominator of the lower-simplex
vertex-averaging law at step \(1/d\). Equivalently, the mean of
the numerator under lower-simplex uniform probability is that
same denominator. Consequently:

* the minimum-coordinate label remains uniform;
* \(t\) keeps its Beta \((1,d-1)\) law;
* \(t\) and \(w\) remain independent within the cell;
* \(w\) has precisely the law of
  \(\rho W+e_J/d\) with \(d-1\) coordinates.

There is no missing cell-probability factor.

## 3. Reconstructed martingale and boundary cases

Apply Section 1 with \(m=d-1\), independently of the label and
of \(t\), to couple this \(w\) outward to a uniform lower-simplex
point \(x_{\mathrm{face}}\). Reconstruct the full vectors using
the same \(i,t\). The output is uniform on that minimum cell;
the uniform choice of label therefore makes it uniform on the
entire simplex.

Conditioned on the actual generating variables \(i,t,W,J\),
the expectation of the output is exactly the input \(Y\).
The tower property yields \(\mathbb E[X\mid Y]=Y\).
This argument does not assume that the original independent
vertex label generating \(Y_b\) is its minimum-coordinate label.
It constructs a new coupling with the required two marginals.

At \(d=2\), the lower simplex is a point. The reconstruction is
the identity coupling, and the critical law itself is uniform
on the interval. The event \(t=1\), tied minima, and simplex
boundary faces are null. None creates an omitted atom.

## 4. Smaller steps and the exact sharp obstruction

For \(0\le b\le1/d\), the pointwise interpolation
\[
Y_b=(1-db)Z+db\,Y_{1/d}
\]
uses the same original \(Z,I\). Jensen followed by the critical
inequality proves the convex-order assertion. Both endpoint
parameters are included.

For \(b\ge1/d\), the minimum is always among the unraised
coordinates, because their minimum is at most
\((1-b)/(d-1)\le b\). For any chosen \(k\) coordinates of a
uniform \(d\)-coordinate simplex point, translation and dilation
give
\[
\Pr(\min Z_i\ge s)=(1-ks)_+^{d-1},\qquad
\mathbb E\min Z_i=1/(dk).
\]
It follows exactly that
\[
\mathbb E\min_i(Y_b)_i=\frac{1-b}{d(d-1)},\qquad
\mathbb E\min_i Z_i=\frac1{d^2}.
\]
For \(b>1/d\), the first is smaller, violating the required
inequality for the continuous concave minimum function.
At the critical value the entire minimum-coordinate distribution,
not just its mean, agrees; the constructed coupling preserves
the minimum and its label pointwise. Hence the stated nonaffine
critical equality examples are correct, and critical strictness
must not be inferred.

## 5. Optional independent-step classification: exact correction

The initial Section 5 uniqueness statement on steps in \([0,1)\)
was false because the zero step preserves uniformity. More
generally, for every \(p\in[0,1]\), the law
\[
p\delta_0+(1-p)m(1-r)^{m-1}\,dr
\]
preserves uniformity in the independent-step construction.
It has
\[
G(x)=p+(1-p)m x\quad(0<x<1).
\]
The summed output density is still one.

For \(m\ge3\), this is also the exact corrected classification.
The identity \(\sum_jG(x_j)=m\) on the open simplex implies
\(G''=0\) distributionally: fix all but three coordinates and
take the mixed derivative in two of the remaining coordinates.
Letting the fixed coordinate total tend to zero gives the result
on all of \((0,1)\). Thus \(G(x)=p+c x\), with
\(p=\Pr(R=0)\), and the density identity gives \(mp+c=m\).
Undoing the weight in the defining Stieltjes integral gives
precisely the mixture above. In particular, imposing
\(\Pr(R=0)=0\) makes the Beta step law unique.

Every such mixture has mean \((1-p)/(m+1)\le1/(m+1)\), so the
intended limitation of the simpler method remains valid.
The \(m=2\) exception is correctly retained: deterministic
step \(1/2\) also preserves uniformity there.

The final source makes only the narrower absolutely continuous
uniqueness claim. In that setting \(G(0)=0\), continuity extends
the density identity to the needed boundary configurations,
and comparing three-coordinate configurations proves
\(G(x)+G(y)=G(x+y)\). Monotonicity then gives \(G(x)=mx\).
This amended proof is valid and requires no general classification
of singular step laws.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
